Implant Comfort

Dental Implant Pain: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options

Understanding why discomfort may develop around a dental implant, the signs to be aware of, and how professional assessment can help identify the most appropriate care.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation — £80Call 020 71833573

✓ Clinical Implant Assessment · ✓ Tailored Treatment Plans · ✓ Experienced Implant Team

Dental implants are designed to function like natural tooth roots, integrating with the jawbone to provide stable, long-lasting support for replacement teeth. For most patients, implants function comfortably and without issue once the healing period is complete.

However, in some cases, patients may experience discomfort or pain around an implant. This discomfort may occur shortly after placement as part of the normal healing process, or it may develop weeks, months, or even years later. The underlying cause can vary — it may involve the surrounding tissues, bite pressure, infection, or a problem with the implant components themselves.

Whatever the timing or nature of the discomfort, professional dental assessment can help determine the underlying cause and identify appropriate treatment options. In many cases, implant pain can be managed effectively once the source has been identified.

Is Dental Implant Pain Normal?

It is quite common for patients to experience mild discomfort during the early healing phase following implant placement. Some tenderness, swelling, or sensitivity around the surgical site is a normal part of the body's healing response and typically subsides within a few days to a couple of weeks.

However, if pain persists beyond the expected healing period, intensifies rather than improves, or develops after a period of comfortable function, this may indicate an underlying issue that warrants investigation. Delayed or persistent pain should always be evaluated by a dental professional, as early assessment can help identify the cause before it progresses.

It is worth noting that the nature, intensity, and timing of implant discomfort can vary considerably between individuals. What one patient experiences may differ from another, which is why clinical evaluation is important for an accurate diagnosis.

Common Causes of Implant Pain

Dental implant pain can arise from a number of different causes. Identifying the specific factor — or combination of factors — is essential for determining the most appropriate treatment approach.

Infection Around the Implant

Bacterial infection of the gum tissue or bone surrounding the implant — known as peri-implant mucositis or peri-implantitis — is one of the most common causes of implant discomfort. Infection may cause swelling, tenderness, and bleeding, and can compromise the supporting structures if left unaddressed.

Bite Pressure or Misalignment

If the implant restoration does not align correctly with the opposing teeth, excessive or uneven bite forces may be transmitted through the implant. This can lead to discomfort during biting or chewing and, over time, may place additional stress on the implant and surrounding bone.

Gum Tissue Inflammation

Inflammation of the soft tissues around the implant can occur independently of infection. Irritation from rough restoration margins, food impaction, or inadequate oral hygiene may contribute to gum tenderness and discomfort in the implant area.

Component Problems & Healing Complications

In some cases, discomfort may arise from a loose or damaged implant component, such as the abutment or crown. Additionally, complications during the bone healing phase — including incomplete osseointegration — may result in ongoing sensitivity or discomfort around the implant site.

Signs and Symptoms of Implant Discomfort

The symptoms associated with dental implant pain can vary between individuals and depend on the underlying cause. Being aware of the signs that may warrant professional evaluation can help patients seek timely advice.

Pain When Biting or Chewing

Discomfort that occurs when pressure is applied through the implant — particularly during eating — may suggest bite misalignment, a loose component, or stress on the surrounding bone.

Swelling or Tenderness

Localised swelling, puffiness, or tenderness of the gum tissue around the implant may indicate inflammation or infection that requires clinical evaluation.

Gum Sensitivity

Heightened sensitivity in the gums surrounding the implant, including discomfort when brushing or touching the area, may be a sign of tissue irritation or early infection.

Persistent Discomfort

Ongoing or recurring discomfort around the implant site — particularly pain that does not resolve with time or that returns after a period of comfort — should be assessed to rule out underlying complications.

Potential Effects on Oral Function

When dental implant pain is left unaddressed, it may begin to affect everyday oral function. Understanding these potential effects can help patients appreciate the value of seeking timely professional assessment.

Chewing ability is often the first function to be affected. Patients may begin to avoid chewing on the side of the painful implant, which can alter eating habits and place additional strain on other teeth. Over time, this compensatory behaviour may contribute to uneven wear or discomfort elsewhere in the mouth.

Bite balance can also be disrupted. If an implant is causing pain due to misalignment or a component issue, the way the upper and lower teeth come together may be affected, potentially contributing to further discomfort or strain on the jaw joints.

In cases where an underlying infection or bone healing complication is responsible for the pain, implant stability itself may be at risk. Early intervention can help address these issues before they progress to a point where more extensive treatment is required.

Perhaps most importantly, persistent implant discomfort can affect overall oral comfort and confidence in the implant. Professional assessment can help restore both function and peace of mind.

Treatment Options for Implant Pain

The most appropriate treatment for dental implant pain depends on the underlying cause, which can only be determined through thorough clinical assessment. A range of approaches may be considered.

Professional Implant Cleaning & Maintenance

If bacterial build-up or early gum inflammation is contributing to discomfort, professional cleaning around the implant may help reduce symptoms. Regular implant maintenance appointments are an important part of ongoing implant care and can help identify issues before they progress.

Adjustment of Bite Alignment

Where bite misalignment is contributing to implant pain, careful adjustment of the implant restoration or opposing teeth may help redistribute bite forces more evenly. This can often be achieved through minor modifications to the implant crown without the need for more extensive treatment.

Treatment of Inflammation or Infection

If gum inflammation or peri-implant infection is identified, targeted treatment may help manage the condition and reduce discomfort. This may involve antimicrobial therapies, improved hygiene protocols, or surgical intervention in more advanced cases.

Repair or Replacement of Implant Components

If a loose, damaged, or worn implant component is responsible for the discomfort, repair or replacement of the affected part may help resolve the issue. In cases where the implant itself has failed, implant replacement or removal may need to be considered following a full assessment.

Treatment options vary depending on the underlying cause. A thorough clinical assessment is required before any treatment plan can be recommended.

Importance of Professional Implant Assessment

Implant discomfort should always be evaluated by a dental professional, regardless of when it develops or how mild it may seem. Pain is the body's way of signalling that something may require attention, and in the context of dental implants, early assessment can make a significant difference to the outcome.

A thorough examination may involve clinical assessment of the gum tissues, probing around the implant to check for pocket depth, and dental imaging to evaluate the condition of the surrounding bone. Implant stability testing may also be carried out to assess whether the implant remains securely integrated with the jawbone.

Early diagnosis of the underlying cause can help prevent more complex complications from developing. What may begin as minor gum inflammation could, if left unaddressed, progress to bone loss or implant instability. Timely professional evaluation helps ensure the most conservative and effective treatment approach is identified.
